title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 The Pope's AI Encyclical: The Most Serious Thinking on AI and Education to Date
author: Bauschard, Stefan
summary: Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica Humanitas on May 25, 2026—a full papal encyclical on AI running to roughly 250 paragraphs that treats artificial intelligence as a civilizational turning point alongside industrial capitalism and the nuclear age. The article reads it through an educational lens, noting first that the contrast between the Church's response (a book-length, philosophically rigorous institutional document) and most schools' response (an acceptable use policy, if anything) is itself revealing of the stakes. Three paragraphs carry special weight for educators: paragraph 92 argues technology is not merely a tool because once it becomes the measure of everything it dictates institutional priorities; paragraph 104 states that AI cannot be considered morally neutral because every system embeds choices about what to measure, ignore, and classify; paragraph 107 delivers a structural critique of alignment—a more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few engineers and executives rather than through broad democratic deliberation. The author identifies educators' specific section of the wall: forming people who can bring judgment and epistemic humility to decisions the technology cannot make, and producing informed users—which the encyclical names as a constitutive component of AI governance alongside laws and regulators. A critical note: paragraph 99's confident metaphysical claims about AI lacking experience and understanding overreaches into territory that serious philosophy of mind considers genuinely unsettled.
points: * Magnifica Humanitas treats AI as a civilizational event comparable to industrial capitalism and the nuclear age—the encyclical form signals that rubrics and policies cannot address challenges of this structural depth. * Paragraph 104 argues AI is not morally neutral: every system embeds choices about what to measure, ignore, and optimize, making the decision to deploy it a moral act before any question of how it is used. * Paragraph 107 delivers a structural critique of alignment: a more moral AI is not enough if values are set by a few engineers and executives rather than through broad democratic deliberation. * Educators hold a specific section of the wall: forming young people who bring judgment, openness, and epistemic humility to decisions the technology cannot make—preserving productive friction against AI's implicit message that thinking is an inefficiency. * The encyclical names informed users as a constitutive component of AI governance alongside laws and regulators; the institution responsible for producing informed users is the school.
quotes: This is not a short statement, a technology policy, or a set of classroom guidelines. It is a major institutional document, running to roughly 250 paragraphs across five chapters, that treats AI as a civilizational turning point — one that will reshape work, truth, power, human dignity, democracy, and the formation of young people.

Technology is not simply a tool. When it becomes the standard by which everything is judged, it begins to dictate what matters and what can be discarded, reducing creation to an object of exploitation and human beings to mere cogs in a system driven toward ever greater efficiency.

We cannot consider AI to be morally neutral. In reality, every technical tool embodies choices and priorities through what it measures, ignores and optimizes, and how it classifies people and situations.
A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few.

The Pope is not asking whether students should be allowed to use ChatGPT on essays and what AI traffic lights to put up. He is asking what happens to human beings when intelligence becomes increasingly artificial, automated, conversational, and concentrated in the hands of a few powerful actors.

Informed users is what an education system produces when it is doing its job in this moment. The encyclical is, in effect, telling us that informed users are a piece of the governance infrastructure of AI, and that the institution responsible for producing them is the school.
The Pope thinks AI is reshaping what it means to be human. Your kid's school thinks AI is mostly a cheating problem. That gap is the real story.
